evidence_set: The authors argue that incomplete distribution during life, including arterial–venous differences, and the variable make-up of blood after death cannot fully explain the large site differences, while allowing incomplete distribution during life as a contributory factor. They propose diffusion after death along concentration gradients from organs holding high drug concentrations, especially liver and lung, into nearby vessels; they state that the cause remains unresolved and is probably multifactorial, with diffusion from solid organs the major proposed factor. The report describes one post-mortem sampling occasion per person, at autopsy, and presents no repeated post-mortem sampling, so the timing and mechanism of the changes are inferred rather than followed directly after death. Case 4 also has a separate blood sample from life.

evidence_set: Of 2,719 deaths suspected before autopsy to be drug-related, 2,454 had a drug-related final cause after full autopsy and comprehensive toxicology and 265 did not; of 237 deaths not suspected, 115 had a drug-related final cause and 122 did not (2,956 deaths, 2016–2021, after excluding people under 18, obvious lethal injuries and suicidal drug overdoses). Editors' calculation: 265 of 2,719 is 9.75%; 115 of 237 is 48.5%. This is a study of drug presence and final cause attribution, not of drug concentrations. Cause assignment by the pathologist is treated as correct, not independently validated.

evidence_set: The review proposes criteria for attributing a death to a drug: exclude other reasonable or competing explanations and establish an understood mechanism, a concentration capable of causing death and a fit with the circumstances. For THC the authors say it may not be possible to provide a minimum blood concentration that might be regarded as causal because of delays from death to sampling; many, if not most, laboratories can detect 1–2 ng/mL in post-mortem blood, and lower values could most likely reflect use days earlier. A blood THC test, rather than urine cannabinoids or history alone, is required to link a death to recent use. The review relays Tormey's discussion as advising that cannabis could be contributory only with use within 2 h of the cardiorespiratory arrest, ideally with blood THC confirmed. The supplied review does not identify Tormey as a coroner, and the cited discussion has not been independently read.
Discussion, 8th–12th paragraphs (p. 304), especially the paragraph beginning “Tormey discusses”; reference 80 (p. 306)

In human bodies sampled more than once, significant falls in femoral-blood THC after death were reported in one study (ref 30), among falls for several other substances; the review gives no effect sizes. Separately, for repeated-sampling studies where the interval was available or estimated, the review reports a mean of 17 h from death to the first sample (range 1–292 h), citing 12 references that do not include the THC study. It supplies no underlying timing values, weights or aggregation method, so that summary cannot be independently recomputed here or assigned to the THC study. Separately, section 5.2 reports higher THC in femoral blood after death than in samples from life (collective refs 30,42), without effect sizes. Antemortem elimination, incomplete absorption/distribution at the earlier sample, possible later drug administration, hospital selection and plasma/serum versus whole-blood differences limit such comparisons; neither a rise nor a fall alone is uniquely attributable to redistribution. The underlying THC articles and any absent supplemental material were not read.
